newsitem.title: UK: "Liberated" Major feels election tide turning.
newsitem.headline: "Liberated" Major feels election tide turning.

text.p: "Let's get rid of this silly barrier!" Prime Minister John Major says, ordering his minders to remove a rope so he can work the crowd more easily.

The gesture is no accident. Major wants to contrast his relaxed meet-the-people style of electioneering with what he sees as the over-choreographed campaign of his rival, Labour leader Tony Blair, where spontaneity has been at a premium.
As well as relishing being freed physically from the London political hothouse, Major says the May 1 election has also liberated him politically.

After months of struggling in parliament with a small majority, constantly cobbling together compromises within his feuding party to survive another vote, he is visibly relieved to be on the stump so he can be himself.

"It's perfectly true to say I feel liberated, in the sense that I can now address the social agenda that I have always cared about," Major told reporters accompanying him on a two-day swing through south-western England.
Critics would say that it is infighting within his own party over Europe that has increasingly distracted Major in his 6-1/2 years as prime minister.
But he blames the aftermath of recession for not being able to devote more energy to turning the 'have-nots' into 'haves', to use a phrase from his stump speech.
"For much of the last parliament I have been politically hamstrung by the need to get the economy right," he said during the interview, conducted on Tuesday.
Several Conservative "Euro-sceptics" have tested Major's patience by openly defying his wait-and-see approach on whether to join the European Union's planned single currency.
Labour claims at least 100 Conservative candidates are openly opposed to the single currency, storing up trouble for Major if the Conservatives win an unprecedented fifth straight term of office.
But he firmly rejects the suggestion that he should run on a clear-cut right-wing, "Euro-sceptic" platform.

"I'm always being told that provided I would be able to do this, to do that, the world would turn on its head. Well, I'm not prepared to turn on my head...People will have to accept me for what I am," he says.
Major bristles at another suggestion that his campaign call for Conservatives to show compassion to the have-nots is electoral opportunism.

"It's hard to say I've suddenly become a One-Nation Conservative when I talked about a classless society when I first went into Downing Street," the prime minister, himself from humble origins, shoots back.
Opinion polls put the Conservatives as much as 21 points behind Labour, but Major believes the tide is turning -- and turning earlier than it did when he came from behind to win the 1992 election.
"The campaign is getting into its stride. I think I can feel the change already... My fingertips suggest there is a change occurring earlier in this election," he says.

Major denies that the attacks he has made on Blair, accusing him of hiding from the press and being panicked into policy U-turns, are personal. Rather, he says he is making an important political point about the qualities of leadership that a prime minister must have.
"It's perfectly legitimate to focus on that...If you are blown around by the wind in opposition when the opinion polls tell you you have a big lead, what would it be like in government?"
Major, who confirmed that he likes to eat Marmite sandwiches to get him through the day, says he can find no time on the road to read anything except his briefing papers.
Nor, he admits, has he kept up with the Spice Girls, Britain's latest chart-topping pop group. Major can name only two of the five.
"Ask me about opera," he says.

Realising that it would not be good politics to brush off millions of Spice Girls fans, Major hurriedly adds: "I think they have done a great deal for British exports and the music industry, but I don't think you boys and girls give me enough time to watch them."
